story.headline: The dollar hit its highest since April 2025 as traders fully priced a December Fed hike and stocks soared on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia. Oil fell below $90 on supply worries.

reads.policy: Traders now fully expect a quarter-point Fed hike in December and see a good chance of another in January. The Bank of England sounds firmer too, and the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan are expected to hike in December. The Fed still looks set to go furthest, which keeps the dollar on top.
reads.growth: Business surveys showed the US economy and UK services slowing in November, while Germany sped up and France shrank. None of it changed what central banks are expected to do, so growth news is taking a back seat to interest rates for now.
reads.inflation: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. New York Fed President John Williams called US inflation simply too high. US core inflation on Wednesday and Australian inflation on Tuesday evening are the week's big tests.
reads.risk: US stocks jumped after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as chief executive, ending last week's selloff. Calmer markets drew money out of the yen and the franc. With fear gone, the dollar rose on interest rates instead.
reads.tot: Oil fell below $90 as more Middle East supply reached the market, which hurts the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers like the euro area and Japan. Gold won back much of last week's fall, which gives the Aussie some support.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: France's debts weigh more now that its economy looks close to recession. Heavy US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which supports the dollar's yield but raises questions about debt over time.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. Traders now fully expect a quarter-point hike in December and see a good chance of another in January.
fed.priced: December: quarter-point hike fully expected. January: another hike more likely than not.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal. New York Fed President John Williams said on Monday, November 23 that inflation is simply too high and the risk to stable prices has grown.
fed.watch: US consumer confidence on Tuesday, November 24 at 9:00 AM CT and core inflation for October on Wednesday, November 25 at 7:30 AM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait. Falling oil adds to the case for patience.
boc.watch: Governor Tiff Macklem speaks Tuesday, November 24 at 11:25 AM CT, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, but a jump in shop sales in the third quarter strengthens the case for one.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures and stronger spending argue for a hike, while unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on Friday, November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is 4.0%, but the euro has slipped to its weakest in about 19 months as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Weak factories and France's debts, which the bank's stability report singled out, limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: Germany's Ifo business mood survey on Tuesday, November 24 at 3:00 AM CT and the accounts of the October meeting on Thursday, November 26 at 6:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Inflation is above its 2% goal, but the dollar still trades near 159 yen because US rates keep rising faster.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2% for a second month, and the weak yen keeps pushing up import and food prices. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: The bank's own core inflation measure on Tuesday, November 24 at 11:00 PM CT, Tokyo's November inflation figures on Thursday, November 26 at 5:30 PM CT, and any sign Japan steps in near 160 yen. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Job losses and a business survey showing the fastest shrinking in more than five years suggest rates have peaked, and the Aussie is near its lowest in a year.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected. Some bets on cuts in 2027 are building.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high for most of the board, but the economy is clearly weakening and firms say price rises are slowing. That makes a further hike unlikely and puts the timing of a first cut in question.
rba.watch: Australian inflation for October on Tuesday, November 24 at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. Chief economist Huw Pill said on Monday, November 23 that the bank must act now on inflation, which makes a second hike in December more likely.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Services are slowing, but Pill pointed to inflation staying above target for most of the past five years.
boe.watch: Policymaker Megan Greene speaks on Tuesday, November 24 at 6:30 AM CT. The Financial Stability Report is Thursday, November 26 at 4:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up in stock markets or the Gulf that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight, and the Bank of England sounds ready to hike again in December. It still trades near a one-year low against the dollar.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. A shrinking economy and job losses suggest those rates have peaked, and it trades near its lowest in a year.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits third on the board. Firm dairy prices and strong shop sales help, but doubts over a December rate hike and a firm US dollar keep it near its lowest in many years.

USD.summary: The dollar sits fourth, in the middle of the board. High US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh. It trades at its highest since April 2025, with a December Fed hike fully expected.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Germany's economy is speeding up, but France is close to recession and its debts hold the euro back. It trades at its weakest in about 19 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. It is near its weakest against the US dollar this year.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike offers some hope, but the dollar trades near 159 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. It gains mainly when fear in markets sends safe-haven money its way.
